newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin firm on land reform, private ownership.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin firm on land reform, private ownership.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin said on Thursday the Russian government must speed up land privatisation and free trade of land, reaffirming his commitment to an important element of economic reforms.

In a document accompanying his state of the nation speech to parliament, Yeltsin ordered the government to work out laws on property rights for non-agricultural land and land-trading by August 1 and to present them to the State Duma lower house.
"We cannot count on serious long-term investment if we do not provide for property rights and market turnover of land," Yeltsin said.
"The government has impermissibly delayed the carrying out of last year's presidential decree on constitutional land rights of citizens."

Yeltsin, who launched Russia on the path to a market economy at the start of 1992, views the abolition of Communist-era land ownership restrictions as essential for economic revival, especially in the ailing farm sector.
Impatient with delays in passing a land code which would guarantee private land ownership, Yeltsin signed a decree last March allowing Russian farmers to buy and sell land.
The decree remains a temporary measure and most of its articles have never been fulfilled. The decree is due to be replaced by a long-awaited land code when it is finally passed.

Last spring the communist-dominated Duma approved a tailored version of the code. But it was a far cry from Yeltsin's draft land code guaranteeing private ownership and including purchase, sale, lease and mortgage.
The State Duma is dominated by communists and agrarians who favour the huge, Soviet-era collective farms.
The Duma's version would permit rental and life-time ownership of agricultural land, but would not let farmers or investors buy, sell or mortgage it.
Yeltsin said he would veto the Duma's draft, and the upper house sent it back to the Duma for review.
The communists who ruled Russia from 1917 banned private ownership of land, which small farmers had enjoyed only from 1861, when the tsars formally abolished serfdom.

In the Soviet era virtually all land was owned by the state after a brutal campaign of collectivisation launched by Soviet dictator Josef Stalin in the 1930s forced private farmers to join huge state farms.
Constitutional changes in 1990 and 1993 offered the right to own land in theory, but these were never cemented into law, and many state farmers still say buying and selling land is wrong.
Collective farms have found it difficult to cope with the new realities of a market economy, and output has slumped well below Soviet-era levels.
Russia's 1996 net grain harvest was the second poor return in a row following 1995 output of 63.5 million tonnes -- the worst in three decades.
Private farms account for less than five percent of Russian farms in Russia, with about 12 million hectares (30 million acres), but their share of output is just over five percent.

At least 12 million people own 132 million hectares (326 million acres) of land, distributed as part of agricultural reforms. Another 50 million families, including city-dwellers, own about 29 million hectares (72 million acres).
